What's your startup worth?

queue.title: 5 reasons your deck won't get a second meeting.
queue.body:
5 reasons your deck won't get a second meeting (from 50+ AU investor conversations):

1. Market size built top-down ("TAM is $50B") with no bottom-up SOM check.
2. Revenue projection that hockey-sticks at month 13 with no triggering event.
3. "AI-powered" mentioned 11 times; the actual moat mentioned zero.
4. Cap table that's already crowded at pre-seed (you sold too cheap, too early).
5. No comparable AU raises in the last 18 months — you're pricing off US bands.

Fix list, in order: (1) ground SOM in 3 customer interviews, (2) tie the hockey-stick to a specific channel unlock, (3) name the moat in 6 words, (4) model the next 2 dilution rounds before raising this one, (5) cite 3 AU comparable raises.

The SVI investor-readiness module scores all 5 in 10 minutes — free at https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: The 30% SME owners lose at exit.
queue.body:
AU SME owners lose 20–40% of their company's value at sale. Three reasons, in order of frequency:

1. **Documentation gap.** Buyers discount aggressively when financials aren't audited and contracts aren't centralised. Median discount: 18%.

2. **Customer concentration.** One customer > 25% of revenue triggers a buyer haircut. Median discount: 12%.

3. **Owner-dependence.** If the owner is in 80% of customer relationships, the buyer prices in attrition. Median discount: 22%.

All three are fixable in 12–18 months — but only if you start measuring before you start selling.

The SVI Business Health Check surfaces all three. Free preview → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: How AU investors actually score private companies.
queue.body:
From 30 conversations with AU pre-seed / seed investors, here's the actual scorecard they run (not the one in their thesis deck):

• Founder quality: 30% weight — founder-market fit + repeat indicator
• Market timing: 20% — why now, not 3 years ago, not 3 years from now
• Channel evidence: 20% — one channel with unit economics that work
• Differentiation: 15% — the 6-word moat
• Capital efficiency: 10% — burn vs hypothesis tested per A$ raised
• Cap table: 5% — clean, no zombie equity

Notice what's missing: TAM, AI usage, team size, fancy advisors.

The SVI weighs the same things — it's literally trained on these conversations.

Score yourself in 10 minutes → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: Your cap table is your story.
queue.body:
Your cap table is your fundraising story whether you wrote it or not.

Things investors read from row 1:
• Founder % at pre-seed: < 70% = you sold too early
• Advisor shares > 2%: someone overpaid for an intro
• Multiple convertible notes with different caps: messy → discount
• ESOP < 10% by Series A: you'll have to top up dilutively
• A friend with 8%: hardest call you'll ever make

Fix them before the data room, not during diligence.

The SVI cap-table module flags all 5 in seconds → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: 7 signals your business is investor-ready.
queue.body:
7 signals your business is actually investor-ready (not just hopeful):

1. You can describe your ICP in one sentence and 3 of your last 5 customers fit it.
2. Your CAC payback is < 18 months and you can prove it from raw data.
3. You have 12 months of monthly cohort retention.
4. Your data room exists today, not 'when needed'.
5. You've turned down at least one deal that didn't fit.
6. Your cap table can absorb 2 more rounds without losing founder control.
7. You know which 3 metrics your investor will index on at the next round — and you're measuring them weekly.

4+ ticked = you're ready to start conversations.
2–3 = 90 days of work first.
0–1 = stay heads-down, don't burn intros.

The SVI investor-readiness module checks all 7 → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: The $10k question every founder must answer at Series A.
queue.body:
At Series A, the partner will ask you ONE question that decides the meeting:

"What's the smallest experiment you could run with $10k that would invalidate this whole thing — and have you run it?"

Founders who answer in < 30 seconds with a specific past experiment + result get a follow-up. Everyone else gets 'great pitch, let's keep in touch'.

Why this question? Because it tests 3 things at once: do you know your riskiest assumption, have you actually de-risked it, and do you have the cheapness instinct that survives the next 7 years.

Write your answer in your phone notes today. Re-read it in 30 days.

The SVI 'experiment hygiene' dimension scores this directly → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: Multiple of EBITDA — 4 ways founders get it wrong.
queue.body:
"My business is worth 5× EBITDA" — every conversation we've had with an SME owner. 4 ways that math is usually wrong:

1. **Wrong multiple.** Service businesses with owner-in-loop trade 1.5–3×, not 5×. Asset-light tech with 12-month retention trades 6–10×.

2. **Wrong EBITDA.** Owner add-backs are real only if the buyer can actually remove them. Personal car, family salaries, one-off contracts — buyers discount these.

3. **Wrong year.** Buyers look at trailing 12 months, not the best year you ever had. If your best year was 2 years ago, you're getting last year's number.

4. **No working capital adjustment.** The price you negotiate isn't the cheque you receive. WC adjustment can move it 5–15%.

The SVI valuation report does all 4 corrections automatically → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: The 13 dimensions SVI scores — and why ARR isn't one.
queue.body:
The Startup Value Index scores 13 dimensions. Conspicuously not on the list: ARR.

Why not? ARR is an output. The 13 dimensions are inputs — the things that produce ARR (or don't).

The 13:
1. Founder quality & founder-market fit
2. Market structure & timing
3. Channel evidence & CAC trajectory
4. Retention & cohort depth
5. Unit economics & contribution margin
6. Capital efficiency (burn vs hypotheses tested)
7. Differentiation & defensibility
8. Cap-table hygiene
9. Governance & founder agreements
10. Customer concentration
11. IP & data moat
12. Operational maturity
13. Capital plan / runway-to-milestone fit

Score high on all 13 and ARR follows. Score high on ARR alone and you're one bad cohort away from a down round.

Free assessment → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: ESOP done wrong: the Division 83A trap.
queue.body:
ESOP done wrong: the Division 83A trap that quietly destroys A$50–200k of employee value.

The scenario: AU startup, pre-seed, founder issues options at A$0.10 strike. 2 years later, raises Series A at A$2.50 per share. Employee exercises.

Without a Division 83A qualifying scheme: employee owes income tax on the A$2.40 gain ON EXERCISE. They don't have cash. They either sell shares (if they can — usually they can't) or skip exercise.

With a Division 83A scheme (eligible startup): tax deferred until sale, not exercise. Employee actually gets the upside.

Most AU founders don't set this up correctly because the lawyer who drafted the constitution didn't structure the ESOP plan rules.

Fix it BEFORE Series A. After the round it's much harder.

ESOP audit module in SVI → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: Quiz: how many of these 7 are true?
queue.body:
Quiz — how many are true for your startup right now?

1. You know your monthly burn to A$1k accuracy.
2. You can name your top 3 customer acquisition channels and rank them by CAC.
3. Your last cohort had > 80% month-1 retention.
4. Your cap table is in a dedicated tool (not a spreadsheet).
5. You've written down what would make you SHUT IT DOWN.
6. You've turned down a customer in the last 90 days because they weren't a fit.
7. Your runway calculation has 3 scenarios, not 1.

Score yourself:
6–7 → you're running this like a CEO. Investors notice.
4–5 → solid. Tighten the rest in 60 days.
2–3 → busy, not running. Pause and instrument.
0–1 → you're hoping, not building. Stop and reset.

Full self-assessment in 10 min → https://startupvalueindex.com

queue.title: One year ago your valuation was X. Now what?
queue.body:
One year ago a generalist VC told you your startup was worth A$8M. You believed it.

This year the market is different. Same revenue. Same team. Same product. New number?

The top 3 reasons valuations move in 12 months (in order of frequency):

1. **Comparable raises shifted.** AU pre-seed in 2025 vs 2026 — different bands. Same company gets a different number purely because the comparables repriced.

2. **Capital intensity changed.** If you can now run on 60% of last year's burn (AI tooling, better channels), your raise size shrinks — and so does your dilution. That's a value INCREASE even with the same headline number.

3. **Evidence depth.** 12 more months of cohort data is worth more than any new feature. A startup with 18 months of retention data trades at a different multiple to one with 6.

The SVI tracks all 3 quarterly. Subscribe to the index → https://startupvalueindex.com
